summary:
We have developed "Mars Orbital Mission", an interactive online simulation game inspired by the 2006 Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) project. In this game, players take on the role of a Flight Director, managing an entire interplanetary campaign across eight distinct stages: from the assembly and launch of a satellite to its insertion into Martian orbit and the execution of its mission to transmit data back to mission control.
This project addresses the challenge of making complex aerospace engineering and orbital mechanics accessible by transforming them into an intuitive, gamified strategic experience. Players must actively balance payload mass, solar energy constraints, and the physics of orbital motion.
This initiative is significant because it bridges the gap between theoretical space science and public education, turning abstract engineering principles into an engaging, hands-on experience that sparks curiosity and nurtures the next generation of STEM learners.
details:
About the project: This is a physics-inspired educational space flight simulation centered on a Mars exploration mission. Initially, your team will be provided with a sum of money from the government to build and develop the project. Players take on the roles of Flight Director, overseeing the entire process, from designing the satellite and selecting launch vehicles to navigating interplanetary trajectories and inserting the craft into a scientific orbit around Mars.

The game is divided into phases that simulate an actual space mission in real-time (Flight Events):

Spacecraft Assembly: Selecting scientific instruments (such as HiRISE, CRISM, CTX, or MARCI) and launch vehicles (e.g., Atlas V-401).

1. Liftoff & Ascent / Max Q.

2. Stage Separation / MECO / Centaur.

3. Parking Orbit (around Earth).

4. Trans-Mars Injection (TMI).

5. Midcourse Correction.

6. Mars Orbit Insertion / Aerobrake.

7. Science Operations / Imaging / Downlink.

In terms of benefits, the game offers educational value and practical experience: it helps players understand the mechanics of deep-space exploration missions, orbital dynamics, and aerospace engineering processes. Besides, it also provides intuitive interaction, transforming complex concepts in physics, mechanics, and engineering into an engaging and accessible gaming experience, all directly within a web browser.

We are committed to carrying out this project with the goal of igniting a passion for STEM: inspiring students and space enthusiasts to delve deeper into science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), with a particular focus on aerospace and astronomy. Furthermore, we aim to promote public scientific literacy by helping the general public understand the complexities, challenges, and meticulous calculations that underpin each of NASA’s actual Mars exploration missions.

About Techniques:

- Web Framework & Technologies: Next.js, HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript/TypeScript.

- Graphics & Simulation: Uses HTML5 Canvas for 2D trajectory simulation, combined with 3D NASA GLB meshes models.

- Deployment platform: Vercel (ensures smooth application performance and supports offline mode)

Our project combines simulation gaming with real-world technical data: it provides a realistic simulation of engineering constraints—such as mass, energy, fairing limits, and vibration risk factors—all packaged within a lightweight, interactive web-based game.

It also features a professional-grade control interface, authentically replicating a Mission Control Center, complete with real-time dashboards, flight event tracking, and dynamic telemetry data.

The team has streamlined physical equations and game thresholds to ensure players aren’t overwhelmed by complex aerospace mathematics, while still preserving the core principles and scientific accuracy.

We have also implemented realistic technical constraints for rockets and spacecraft:

Payload Mass: Must remain within the limits specified for the launch vehicle.

Fairing Envelope & Dynamic Pressure: Ensuring the spacecraft structure can withstand aerodynamic drag during liftoff.

Electrical Power Balance: The power generated by solar arrays must meet the consumption demands of the onboard scientific instruments.

Operational Risk Factor: Accounting for phenomena such as micro-vibrations that may occur when multiple scientific instruments (e.g., HiRISE and CRISM) are operating simultaneously.

We undertook this project with the goal of making specialized knowledge in space science which can otherwise be quite difficult to grasp more accessible through the experience of playing a game. We sincerely thank everyone who has engaged with our project, and we would greatly appreciate any feedback you might have.
